vignette:
Maya's Story

Maya sits with her hands folded in her lap, her calloused palms facing upward-evidence of twelve years spent in construction. She's a foreman on residential projects across the city, the kind of woman who can read blueprints and manage crews with equal competence. Her husband calls her the strongest person he knows. She doesn't feel strong anymore.

Three years ago, at thirty-three, Maya was diagnosed with acute leukemia. The diagnosis came suddenly, almost casually, during what she thought was routine bloodwork for persistent fatigue. She remembers the oncologist's face, the way he didn't quite meet her eyes when he said the word "cancer." She remembers thinking about the foundation she was pouring that week, how the concrete was already set, how you can't go back once it hardens.

The treatment was brutal. Six months of chemotherapy that left her bald, nauseated, and terrified in ways she couldn't articulate to anyone. She'd spent her life in control-controlling job sites, controlling timelines, controlling outcomes. The illness took all of that away. Her body became a battleground she couldn't manage, couldn't negotiate with, couldn't force into compliance. She went into remission after eighteen months of treatment, and the doctors called it a success. Maya calls it the day everything changed.

Now, three years later, she's back at work full-time. She's back at home with her husband Reza and their two teenagers. To most people, she's recovered. But Maya knows better.

She wakes most mornings at 3 a.m., her heart racing, convinced something is wrong with her body. A slight headache becomes a brain tumor. Fatigue means the cancer is back. She's had three emergency room visits in the past year-all false alarms, all leaving her more ashamed than relieved. Her hands shake when she reads health articles, which she does obsessively, sometimes for hours late into the night when sleep won't come.

The construction site, once her sanctuary, has become a minefield of triggers. When a coworker mentions his father's cancer diagnosis, Maya has to excuse herself to the porta-potty where she sits alone, breathing hard, unable to shake the feeling that she's back in the hospital. She's hypervigilant about her health in ways that feel both necessary and suffocating. She checks her lymph nodes regularly, sometimes multiple times a day. She's researched every possible late-effect of chemotherapy, every possible recurrence statistic.

Her relationships are strained. Reza tries to be supportive, but he's tired of the reassurance-seeking, tired of her insistence on going to medical appointments alone because she can't bear his hopeful face. Her teenagers tiptoe around her, unsure whether their mother will be present and engaged or distant and preoccupied. She's missed some of their events because the anxiety about her health felt too overwhelming to leave the house.

What troubles Maya most is the loss of her sense of invulnerability. She used to believe that hard work and discipline could protect her, could ensure things would go according to plan. The illness shattered that belief completely. Now she lives in a world that feels fundamentally unsafe, where her body is a traitor and the future is unknowable. She's survived cancer, yes-but survival, she's discovered, is a much more complicated thing than simply being alive.
